extracted.intended_audience: law students, judges, and practitioners in copyright and publishing law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when literary materials (letters, compilations, abridgments, translations, notes, periodicals, and works of calculation) are protected by copyright or subject to equitable relief, and how to detect piracy or lawful copying. Covers standards courts use (originality, copying, substantial similarity, contract/confidence, and scope of protection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private letters generally not literary works
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters written on private subjects (business or personal intercourse) which were never intended to be published cannot be considered literary compositions entitled to copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts of Equity may sometimes interpose to stop publication of such letters, the basis is not copyright but breach of contract or confidence, or where publication is intended as a source of profit at the risk of wounding private feelings. Examples: injunctions granted where there was agreement not to publish and payment was made; courts reluctant to protect merely because proof of facts would be impeded if letters were treated as copyright material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable relief requires contract/confidence or improper intent
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction to restrain publication of private letters is appropriate on the principle of breach of contract or confidence, or where publication is intended for profit and likely to wound private feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant denies confidence and avows a non-profit vindicatory purpose, equity may dissolve an injunction (example: injunction obtained on account of alleged agency/confidence was dissolved when answer denied confidence and avowed vindication). A 'naked' bill not stating subject, nature, or intended sale/value of letters is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: No monopoly in general subjects; copyright in particular expression/result
rubrics_metrics.description: While general subjects are open to all, each original particular treatise on a general subject is protected: copyright exists only in the result of each author's labour, not in the general subject-matter itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two authors work on same subject and produce similar works, each is entitled to full power over his own book provided there is no copying from the former work. Priority of publication does not necessarily affect property in a later distinct production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compilations: originality in arrangement/exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilations on general subjects are protected when the author exhibits a new and distinct idea in the exposition or arrangement; protection is in the result/arrangement produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the later work is substantially the same scheme of exhibition as the earlier one (merely reprinted with differences not amounting to a fundamental change), the law ought to interfere. Lord Thurlow required examination whether the latter differed sufficiently to be a new and original work.

rubrics_metrics.name: No copying from a former work (compilation piracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must not be any copying from a former work for a compilation to be original; servile transcription of another's compilation is actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Longman (copying of nine-tenths led to verdict), Kearsley (transcribed much but added original matter and corrections and was nonsuited). The test is whether substantial verbatim copying of added material exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronologies/series: focus on whether one is imitation of other
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering piracy of chronological series, the question is whether one work is an imitation (adopting the other's arrangement with merely colourable alterations) or as original as the subject admits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal copying of many consecutive pages (e.g., pages 20–34) was held to support recovery. The nature of the subject (facts that must be related) limits originality but copying the arrangement or text is actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calendars/lists: no general copyright in bare lists, but protection against servile copying
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of names as a general subject cannot ordinarily attract copyright, but an individual compiled calendar or list may have copyright if it is the original labour of the compiler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a later work is merely a transcript with colourable variations, injunction will issue because such materials are often transitory; examples include India Calendars, Court Calendars, Directories—anyone may make these, but servile copying of an existing compilation is restrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries/encyclopedias: limits on quotation and taking of large portions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries and encyclopedias are general subjects and may contain much borrowed material, but there are limits: taking very large portions of a single work implies piracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encyclopaedias or dictionaries extract very large portions (e.g., 75 out of 118 pages from a fencing work), courts have found piracy. The law fixes limits to transcripts so encyclopaedias do not sweep up all modern works and destroy original literary property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps/charts classified as engravings for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps and charts, once doubted as copyright subjects, are included among Engravings and treated under that division of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See relevant chapter on Engravings; historical uncertainty noted but current position includes maps/charts among protected engravings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books of calculations: originality despite identical content if correct
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of calculations (almanacks, logarithms, tables of interest) will necessarily contain the same results if correctly made, yet each work may have copyright as the produce of the labour and ingenuity of its author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piracy is proven by evidence such as copying of the original's mistakes and errors, use of parts of the first work at the press while printing the second, or manuscript alterations being merely colourable. Unusual coincidences (e.g., identical non-alphabetical orderings) can be strong presumptive evidence of copying. Defendants may prove independent calculation to show originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abridgments: must be fair, real, and preserve sense
rubrics_metrics.description: An abridgment is lawful and may receive copyright if it is a fair and real abridgment that preserves the whole in its sense and shows invention, learning, and judgment in retrenching unimportant material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abridgment that merely republishes only part, colourably shortens by transposing or omitting parts, or copies the terms of the facts verbatim may be enjoined. Courts examine and compare both works; example: Newberry's abridgment of Hawkesworth was accepted as meritorious; injunction refused where only one-tenth was abstracted but the narrative (not morale) was taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of quotation: substantial taking implies piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount and substance of quoted material matters; when large portions of a work are taken into a compilation/encyclopaedia or abridgment, an intention to pirate is implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: encyclopaedia taking most of a work's pages held piracy. The principle recurs across compilations, dictionaries, and abridgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations: translators acquire copyright as original works
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator who employs time and abilities in translating classical or foreign-language works justly acquires copyright in their translations; translations are original and protected by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations of works written in Latin (or other languages) by a British subject have been held protected. Although periodical practice sometimes treated translations as public property, courts (Lord Chancellor) have granted injunctions where translations were original and protected by statute (stat. 8 Ann. c.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes and additions to old works acquire separate copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: New notes, additions, annotations, and verbal corrections to an established work, if showing sufficient talent, ingenuity and judgment, acquire a separate copyright distinct from the original text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will grant injunctions to restrain printing of notes published with a new edition. Example: person enjoined from printing Paradise Lost with Dr. Newton's notes. However, these new notes do not confer the right to print the original work when the original is still under someone else's exclusive privilege (e.g., king's printer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's verbal corrections and editorial work protected
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal corrections and alterations made by a critic in preparing an edition (e.g., textual corrections, emendations) are protectable as the critic's copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cited: Dr. Bentley's published corrections were held to confer copyright in those alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical publications: examine manner and substance, not merely contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection of periodical publications depends on the laws regulating the manner of publication; when the manner of presentation or substance of matter deprives a proprietor of control over the work, courts must examine the substance to determine whether protection is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not only the matter (content) that is relevant but how it is given to the public; where publication would entirely deprive proprietor of control over a work the courts may be reluctant to protect. The court must notice and examine the substance of the work itself.
